file() reads the contents of config.json as a plain string of text; jsondecode() then parses that string as JSON and turns it into an HCL structure (map/object/list), whose fields can be accessed with dot notation (local.parsed.region)
The combination only works with files inside modules registered in the Terraform Registry
jsondecode() requires the file to have a .json extension, otherwise it will throw a compile-time error before even reading it
explanation: file(path) reads a file's contents as a string (with no interpretation of format at all). jsondecode(string) parses the given string as JSON and returns the corresponding HCL value — this combination is typical for loading external configuration (e.g., a JSON file with per-environment parameters) into Terraform without hardcoding values in the .tf code itself.

question:
Given the code:
```
resource "aws_launch_template" "app" {
  user_data = base64encode(templatefile("${path.module}/init.sh.tpl", { app_port = var.app_port }))
}
```
Why is base64encode() used on top of the templatefile() result here?
options: base64encode() is required because templatefile() itself always returns data already in binary form

The user_data argument of aws_launch_template (like many other AWS resources expecting user data) must be passed base64-encoded — this is a requirement of the AWS API itself (EC2 expects user data to be base64), not a Terraform quirk; templatefile() returns a plain text string (the rendered template), which needs to be encoded before being passed along
base64encode() is used to encrypt the contents of user_data from prying eyes
Without base64encode(), templatefile() would throw a type validation error
explanation: templatefile(path, vars) reads a template file, substitutes the given variables, and returns the result as a plain string. Some arguments of cloud resources (in particular, user_data for EC2/launch templates) must be passed base64-encoded, per the API's own requirement — hence the templatefile() result is additionally wrapped in base64encode(); this is unrelated to encryption and purely about the format expected by the API.

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  cert_exists = fileexists("${path.module}/certs/custom.pem")
  cert_pem    = local.cert_exists ? file("${path.module}/certs/custom.pem") : null
}
```
Why is the fileexists() function used here before calling file()?
options: fileexists() has no effect on the code — it's just a redundant check with no practical purpose

fileexists() checks whether a file exists at the given path and returns a boolean (true/false) WITHOUT erroring — this allows safely avoiding a call to file(), which would fail with an error if the certificate file is missing (for example, in environments where a custom certificate isn't required)
fileexists() automatically creates the file if it doesn't exist
fileexists() only works with files inside modules from the Terraform Registry
explanation: fileexists(path) is a safe existence check for a file, returning true/false without an error. This allows writing defensive code: first check whether the file exists, and only if it does, call file() (which would itself fail if the file were missing); otherwise, fall back to a default value (e.g., null).

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  script_path = "${path.module}/scripts/deploy.sh"
  dir_only    = dirname(local.script_path)
  file_only   = basename(local.script_path)
}
```
What will local.dir_only and local.file_only be?
options: dir_only = "deploy.sh", file_only = "<path.module>/scripts" — the functions are swapped
dir_only = "<path.module>/scripts" (the directory, without the file name), file_only = "deploy.sh" (just the file name, without the directory path) — same as the Unix dirname/basename commands
Both variables get the same value — the full path as a whole
An error, since dirname()/basename() only work with absolute paths (starting with /)
explanation: dirname(path) returns the path to the directory containing the file (without the file name itself), while basename(path) returns only the file name (the last path component) without the directory. The names and behavior of these functions mirror the identically named Unix utilities dirname/basename.

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  azs           = ["eu-west-1a", "eu-west-1b", "eu-west-1c"]
  primary_az    = element(local.azs, 0)
  wrapped_az    = element(local.azs, 5)
}
```
What does element(local.azs, 5) return, if the list contains only 3 elements (indices 0-2)?
options: An 'index out of range' error, since index 5 is beyond the bounds of the list
"eu-west-1c" (the element at index 5 % 3 = 2) — element() uses cyclic (wrap-around) indexing modulo the length of the list, rather than throwing an error when the index is out of range
null — element() returns null for indices beyond the bounds of the list
An empty string ""
explanation: element(list, index) is a special function: when the index exceeds the list length, it does NOT throw an error, but instead 'wraps around' modulo the list length (5 % 3 = 2 → the third element, index 2). This distinguishes it from regular indexing via square brackets list[5], which would result in an out-of-bounds error.

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  full_list  = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]
  middle_two = slice(local.full_list, 1, 3)
}
```
What will local.middle_two be?
options: ["a", "b", "c"] — slice() includes both boundaries
["b", "c"] — slice(list, start, end) returns the sub-list from index 'start' (inclusive) to index 'end' (NOT inclusive), similar to Python slices
["c", "d"] — slice() counts indices from the end of the list
An error, since slice() requires exactly one numeric argument
explanation: slice(list, start_index, end_index) returns the elements from position start_index inclusive up to end_index NOT inclusive (a half-open interval) — slice(["a","b","c","d","e"], 1, 3) gives ["b", "c"] (indices 1 and 2).

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  priority_order = ["critical", "high", "medium", "low"]
  display_order  = reverse(local.priority_order)
}
```
What will local.display_order be?
options: ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"] — reverse() flips the order of the list's elements
["critical", "high", "medium", "low"] — reverse() does not change the original order, only the type
["low", "high", "medium", "critical"] — reverse() only swaps the first and last elements
An error — reverse() only applies to strings, not to lists
explanation: reverse(list) returns a new list with the elements in the opposite order to the original — a simple and frequently used function, for example when constructing a display order of priorities or a chronology.

options: [22, 80, 443, 8080] for numbers — sorted by numeric value; for strings, sort() sorts in lexicographic (alphabetical) order
sort() only works with strings; for a list of numbers, the code would trigger a type-validation error
[8080, 443, 80, 22] — sort() sorts in descending order, not ascending
The order will remain unchanged, since sort() requires an explicit sort key
explanation: sort(list) returns a new list sorted in ascending order — for numbers this means numeric order ([22, 80, 443, 8080]), for strings, lexicographic (alphabetical) order. The function does not directly support descending sort (for that, combine with reverse(sort(...))).

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  names = ["web", "api", "worker"]
  ips   = ["10.0.1.1", "10.0.1.2", "10.0.1.3"]
  name_to_ip = zipmap(local.names, local.ips)
}
```
What does zipmap(local.names, local.ips) return?
options: A map where the elements of the first list become keys and the correspondingly positioned elements of the second list become values: { "web" = "10.0.1.1", "api" = "10.0.1.2", "worker" = "10.0.1.3" }
An error, if both lists are not sorted the same way
A combined list of all elements from both lists one after another
explanation: zipmap(keys_list, values_list) builds a map, matching elements from two lists by position: the first element of the keys list to the first element of the values list, and so on. Both lists must be of the same length.

options: keys() will return ["name", "region", "size"] (the list of map keys in lexicographic order), values() will return ["web-01", "eu-west-1", "t3.micro"] (the list of values, ordered the same way as the keys, not in the order they were declared in the code)
keys() and values() return the same thing — the entire map as a list
keys() returns the number of keys (a number), not the keys themselves
The order of keys/values always matches the order the fields were declared in the code, not alphabetical order
explanation: keys(map) returns the list of a map's keys, values(map) returns the list of corresponding values; both lists are guaranteed to be ordered consistently with each other, but the order is sorted by keys (lexicographically), not by the order the fields were declared in the original map.

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  all_subnets = ["subnet-1", "subnet-2", "subnet-3", "subnet-4", "subnet-5"]
  batches     = chunklist(local.all_subnets, 2)
}
```
What will local.batches be?
options: ["subnet-1", "subnet-2"] — chunklist() only returns the first chunk of the given size

[["subnet-1", "subnet-2"], ["subnet-3", "subnet-4"], ["subnet-5"]] — chunklist() splits the original list into sub-lists of the given maximum size; the last sub-list may be shorter if the elements don't divide evenly
5 — chunklist() only returns the count of resulting groups
An error, since 5 elements does not divide evenly into groups of 2
explanation: chunklist(list, chunk_size) splits a list into several sub-lists of a given maximum size — the last group may contain fewer elements if the total count isn't a multiple of the chunk size. Useful, for example, for batch-processing a large list of resources in parts.

question:
Given the code:
```

  raw_tags   = ["prod", "", "critical", "", "eu"]
  clean_tags = compact(local.raw_tags)
}
```
What will local.clean_tags be?
options: ["prod", "", "critical", "", "eu"] — compact() does not change a list of strings
["prod", "critical", "eu"] — compact() removes all empty string elements ("") from a list of strings
5 — compact() returns the count of non-empty elements
["prod", "critical", "eu", "", ""] — compact() moves empty strings to the end of the list
explanation: compact(list_of_strings) removes all empty strings ("") from a list — it only works with lists of strings. Useful after operations such as a for-expression with a conditional empty-string substitution instead of null, to then strip out the 'empty placeholders' from the result.

question:
Given the code:
```
locals {
  base_tags  = ["managed-by-terraform"]
  extra_tags = ["prod", "critical"]
  all_tags   = concat(local.base_tags, local.extra_tags, ["eu-west-1"])
}
```
What will local.all_tags be?
options: ["managed-by-terraform", "prod", "critical", "eu-west-1"] — concat() sequentially joins any number of lists into one
An error, since concat() accepts no more than two lists at a time
A list of nested lists: [["managed-by-terraform"], ["prod", "critical"], ["eu-west-1"]]
concat() only works with lists of equal length
explanation: concat(list1, list2, ..., listN) merges any number of lists into a single flat list, preserving order — lists of different lengths and origins (locals, variables, literals) can be combined in a single call.

options: Returns the list of all boolean values unchanged

Returns true only if ALL elements of the given list are true (equivalent to a logical AND over the list) — if even one element is false, the result is false; there is also the opposite function anytrue(), which returns true if at least ONE element is true
Counts the number of true values in the list
alltrue() only works with lists of exactly two elements
explanation: alltrue(boolean_list) is a logical AND over all elements of the list (true if all elements are true). anytrue(boolean_list) is a logical OR (true if at least one element is true). Handy for collapsing several conditions (for example, a compliance checklist) into a single boolean result without manually writing a chain of &&.

question: What is the terraform apply -parallelism=5 flag used for?
options: Limits the number of MODULES that can be applied simultaneously to 5

Limits the number of resources Terraform can create/change/delete SIMULTANEOUSLY (in parallel) during apply — the default is 10; lowering the value is useful if the provider starts returning rate-limiting errors due to too many concurrent API requests
Sets the number of retry attempts on a provider request failure
Defines the number of Terraform CLI worker processes started on the local machine
explanation: -parallelism=N limits the number of resource operations (create/update/delete) Terraform performs in parallel during apply/destroy (the default is 10). Reducing parallelism is a standard way to mitigate rate-limiting errors from a cloud provider when a large number of resources are being changed at once.

question: An engineer runs terraform plan and gets an error: 'Error acquiring the state lock... Lock Info: ID: xxx, Who: ci-runner-42@...'. The previous process holding the lock was killed several hours ago and is definitely no longer running. Which command is designed specifically to resolve this situation?
options: terraform state rm — removes a resource from the state, which releases the lock

terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> — forcibly releases a 'stuck' state lock, using the lock ID from the error message; the command requires confirmation and should be used carefully, only when it's certain the process holding the lock is no longer running
terraform init -reconfigure — reinitializes the backend and automatically releases any locks
You should just wait — Terraform automatically releases the lock after a fixed timeout (15 minutes by default)
explanation: terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> is a command specifically designed to release an 'orphaned' state lock (when the process that acquired the lock terminated abnormally without properly releasing it). It requires an explicit lock ID (from the error message) and interactive confirmation — it should only be used after verifying that no other process is currently actually working with that state, otherwise you risk a concurrent write and state corruption.

question:
A CI pipeline initialization uses:
```
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=prod-tf-state" \
  -backend-config="key=app/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=eu-west-1"
```
while the .tf file itself declares only an empty `backend "s3" {}` block. What is this combination (partial configuration) used for?
options: This is a configuration error — the backend block must always contain all arguments directly in the .tf file

Partial configuration allows not hardcoding specific backend values (bucket/key/region, etc.) in the .tf file, and instead passing them dynamically at init time via -backend-config — convenient when the same configuration is used in different environments/accounts with different backend settings, without changing the code
-backend-config only works with the local backend type, not with s3
Values from -backend-config are completely ignored if a backend block is already present in the code, even if it's empty
explanation: Terraform supports 'partial configuration' for backends — the backend block in code can be declared without some (or all) of its arguments, and the missing values are supplied via -backend-config flags during terraform init (or via a separate backend configuration file). This is a common CI/CD pattern for avoiding hardcoded backend infrastructure details directly in version-controlled code.

question: A configuration directory contains the files terraform.tfvars, dev.auto.tfvars, and secrets.tfvars. An engineer simply runs `terraform plan` without any -var-file flags. Which of these files will Terraform automatically pick up and apply?
options: All three files will be loaded automatically, regardless of their name

terraform.tfvars and dev.auto.tfvars will be loaded automatically (the file terraform.tfvars and any files with a .auto.tfvars/.auto.tfvars.json suffix are picked up without explicit specification); secrets.tfvars will NOT be loaded automatically — it must be explicitly passed via -var-file=secrets.tfvars
Only terraform.tfvars — every other .tfvars file always requires an explicit -var-file
No file will be loaded without an explicit -var-file, regardless of its name
explanation: Terraform automatically loads variables from the file terraform.tfvars (if present) and from ANY files with the .auto.tfvars or .auto.tfvars.json extension in the current directory — without needing to explicitly pass them via -var-file. Any file with a different name (like secrets.tfvars in the example) is ignored by automatic loading and must be passed explicitly via -var-file=<name>.

question:
A CI script uses the following construct:
```
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode
EXIT_CODE=$?
if [ $EXIT_CODE -eq 2 ]; then
  echo "There are changes, apply is required"
fi
```
What do exit codes 0, 1, and 2 mean when using the -detailed-exitcode flag?
options: 0 = there are changes, 1 = an error, 2 = no changes — same as a regular plan

0 = plan completed successfully and there are NO changes (the infrastructure fully matches the code); 1 = an error occurred while running plan; 2 = plan completed successfully and there ARE changes pending apply — this code lets a CI pipeline programmatically distinguish 'nothing to do' from 'apply needed' without parsing the text output
The exit codes are identical to a regular plan without the flag; the flag only affects the format of the text output
0 = success regardless of whether there are changes, 1 = warnings, 2 = critical errors
explanation: Without -detailed-exitcode, terraform plan returns only 0 (success) or 1 (error), regardless of whether there are changes — this is not enough to automate the decision of 'is apply needed or not'. With -detailed-exitcode, a third code is added: 2 means 'the plan was computed successfully and contains changes' — this code is typically what CI logic for 'request approval for apply' is built on, as opposed to 0 ('everything is in sync, apply is not needed').

question:
Given the code:
```
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  for_each      = toset(["blue", "green"])
  ami           = "ami-12345"
  instance_type = "t2.micro"
}
```
How do you correctly reference the id attribute of specifically the "blue" instance from elsewhere in the configuration (for example, in an output)?
options: aws_instance.web[0].id — as with count
aws_instance.web["blue"].id — with for_each over a string set/map, each instance is addressed by its string key in square brackets, not by a numeric index
aws_instance.web.blue.id — dot notation, as if accessing an object field
aws_instance.web.id — for_each does not require specifying a particular instance when accessing attributes
explanation: Resources created via for_each (unlike count) are addressed by string key in square brackets: resource_type.name["key"].attribute. This is a key syntactic difference from count, where addressing uses a numeric index (resource_type.name[0].attribute).

question: An engineer needs to apply changes only to one specific module (e.g., database) within a large configuration, without touching the rest of the resources. Which command correctly limits apply to just that module?
options: terraform apply -target=module.database — -target supports addressing not only individual resources but also entire modules: changes will be applied to ALL resources inside module.database (and their dependencies), but not to the rest of the configuration
terraform apply --module=database — a special flag specifically for selecting a module
-target only works with individual resources and cannot reference an entire module — every resource in the module would have to be listed separately
terraform apply -only database/
explanation: -target can be specified in the form module.<name>, which limits the apply/plan/destroy operation to all resources inside the given module (including its nested modules) and their dependencies — there's no need to list every resource individually. Like a regular resource-level -target, this is a tool for exceptional situations, not for regular practice.

question: What is the required_version argument (e.g., required_version = ">= 1.5.0") used for inside the terraform {} block?
options: Sets the default AWS provider version to be used

Sets a minimum (or otherwise constrained) allowed version of the Terraform CLI itself, under which this configuration is guaranteed to work correctly — if the installed CLI's version doesn't satisfy the constraint, Terraform immediately fails with an error on any command (init/plan/apply), instead of trying to run the operation with a potentially incompatible version
Automatically upgrades the installed Terraform CLI to the required version on the next init
required_version only affects warnings in the output but does not block command execution
explanation: required_version inside the terraform {} block sets a version constraint for the Terraform engine's CLI itself (as opposed to required_providers, which constrains provider versions). If the installed CLI's version doesn't match the constraint, Terraform stops immediately with a clear error, preventing a configuration from accidentally being applied with an incompatible engine version (for example, one using syntax unavailable in an older version).

question: Opening the terraform.tfstate file directly (generally not recommended, but useful for understanding the structure), an engineer sees the field "serial": 47 at the top level of the JSON. What does this field mean?
options: The sequence number of the current Terraform CLI version that created the state

A counter that increases by 1 with every successful state change (for example, after apply) — used by the backend (especially a remote one with locking) to detect conflicts: if someone tries to write a state with a lower serial than what's already saved (i.e., based on an outdated version), this signals a potential race condition or lost update
The number of resources managed by the current state
A unique identifier of the organization in HCP Terraform
explanation: serial is a monotonically increasing version counter, incremented on every change. Remote backends use it (together with lineage) to protect against writing an outdated version of state over a newer one — if an engineer manually pulled the state, edited it, and tried to 'push' it back with the old serial, the backend can detect this as a version conflict.

question: The same state file also has a field "lineage": "a1b2c3d4-..." (a UUID). What is this field used for, and what happens if you try to run terraform state push with a file whose lineage differs from the current state in the backend?
options: lineage is just UI metadata that doesn't affect operation execution

lineage is a unique 'lineage' identifier for a specific state file, assigned when it is first created and unchanged by normal operations; if the lineage of the file being uploaded doesn't match the lineage already stored in the backend, Terraform treats this as a sign that a state from a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT, unrelated configuration is being uploaded, and by default refuses to perform the push, protecting against accidental state substitution
lineage is the identifier of the AWS account in which the infrastructure is created
lineage automatically synchronizes across all workspaces of one organization
explanation: lineage is a UUID generated once when a new state is created (and not changed by normal applies). This is a protective mechanism: if you try to state push a file with a different lineage, Terraform interprets this as an attempt to upload state from an unrelated configuration (rather than a newer/older version of THAT SAME configuration) and blocks the operation by default — preventing a catastrophic mistake of 'overwriting one project's state with a completely different one's state'.

options: external allows running literally any program and getting its arbitrary text output as a string

external runs the specified external program and expects it to return a VALID JSON object in stdout (flat, with string values only) — this allows integrating logic into Terraform that is hard or impossible to express with built-in HCL functions (for example, calling a custom script to get a git SHA), but it requires strict compliance with the expected output format
external only works with programs written in Go, since it uses the same protocol as the providers themselves
The result of the external data source cannot be used elsewhere, only in an output
explanation: data "external" is a universal 'bridge' for integrating arbitrary external logic: the specified program receives JSON via stdin (optionally, via query) and MUST print a correct JSON object with a flat structure (a map of string→string) to stdout — otherwise Terraform will fail with a parsing error. The result is available via data.external.<name>.result.<key>. It's used as an escape hatch when built-in functions/providers aren't enough, but, like provisioners, it's considered a 'last resort' tool due to the lack of type safety and portability.

options: Creates a new HTTP endpoint, accessible externally, to receive webhooks

Performs an HTTP GET request to the given URL during plan/apply and exposes the response body (via the response_body attribute) and the status code — often combined with jsondecode() if the response is in JSON format, to pull dynamic data from an external API directly into the configuration
The http data source can only be used for requests to the HashiCorp Registry itself, not to arbitrary URLs
Data from the http data source is automatically cached forever and never re-requested, even on a repeated plan
explanation: data "http" performs an HTTP request (GET by default) to the given url and exposes response_body (the response body as a string) as well as response_headers/status_code. Combining it with jsondecode() allows extracting structured data from a JSON API directly during plan/apply — useful, for example, for dynamically determining the latest available version of something. It's worth noting that such a request is made on every plan, which can affect reproducibility and execution time.

options: terraform_data and null_resource are two independent, unrelated mechanisms with no shared history

terraform_data — built into Terraform itself (does not require declaring the hashicorp/null provider) — is a placeholder resource for storing arbitrary data and for triggering provisioners/replace_triggered_by; it is officially intended as the modern replacement for null_resource, adding, in particular, a built-in input argument instead of needing to set up a separate triggers map
terraform_data can only be used inside HCP Terraform, while null_resource can only be used in the CLI-driven workflow
terraform_data completely removes the need for provisioners, replacing them with its own internal logic
explanation: terraform_data (starting with Terraform 1.4) is a resource built into the Terraform core (unlike null_resource, which requires the hashicorp/null provider), intended for the same scenarios: storing arbitrary values, attaching provisioners to a change in data, being used as a target for replace_triggered_by. It doesn't eliminate the need for provisioners as a mechanism, but simply provides a more modern built-in 'attachment point' for them.

options: The provisioner runs on EVERY apply regardless of triggers — triggers have no meaning here

The provisioner runs again (via a resource recreation) only if at least one value in the triggers map has changed — here that happens if the content of app.zip or config.json has changed (which is reflected in their MD5 hash via filemd5()); if the file contents have not changed, null_resource and its provisioner are not recreated
The provisioner runs only once, on the first terraform apply, and never again, regardless of triggers
triggers determine HOW MANY SECONDS after apply the provisioner will run, not the condition for recreation
explanation: null_resource (and, similarly, terraform_data via input) has no attributes of its own that reflect real infrastructure, so the triggers mechanism (an arbitrary map) is used as an explicit signal for 'what counts as a change': when ANY value in the triggers map changes, the resource is marked for recreation, which causes the provisioner to run again. Here, filemd5() recomputes a file's hash on every plan, and if the contents of app.zip/config.json have changed, the hash changes, the triggers change, the resource gets recreated, and the provisioner reruns.

options: self refers to the provider handling this resource

Inside a provisioner block, self is a reference to the attributes of the CURRENT resource (aws_instance.web) that this provisioner is attached to — it allows referencing its attributes (id, public_ip, etc.) without having to write the resource's full address, which is especially important since some attributes (e.g., id) only become known during the creation of that very resource
self is a reference to the previous resource in the dependency graph, in execution order
self is only available inside a "local-exec" provisioner, not inside remote-exec
explanation: self, in the context of a provisioner (or a connection block), is a special reference to the attributes of the very same resource that the provisioner belongs to. This is necessary because a provisioner is logically 'embedded' inside a resource's definition, and referencing its own attributes directly by the usual address (aws_instance.web.id inside aws_instance.web) would be redundant/circular — self solves this problem.

options: No difference at all, all is just a synonym for 'list all of the resource's existing attributes'

ignore_changes = all completely disables change tracking for ABSOLUTELY ANY attribute of this resource after its initial creation — Terraform will no longer propose any update changes for it in the plan, unlike a list of specific attributes, where change tracking for the remaining (unlisted) attributes continues to work as usual
ignore_changes = all only works with tags, not with other attributes
ignore_changes = all is automatically applied only to sensitive attributes of the resource
explanation: ignore_changes = all is a special keyword (not a list of attributes) that completely 'freezes' a resource with respect to the update diff after the first apply: changes to ANY attributes (even ones not explicitly listed) will no longer be shown by Terraform as a diff. This is usually used when a resource is entirely managed by an external process after its initial creation via Terraform (for example, a resource with autoscaling that changes its own attributes).

question:
Starting with Terraform 1.8, it became possible to declare provider-defined functions. Given the usage example:
```
locals {
  cidr_info = provider::aws::arn_parse(var.some_arn)
}
```
How are provider-defined functions fundamentally different from built-in HCL functions (such as cidrsubnet(), merge(), etc.)?
options: There's no real difference in usage, only a different call syntax with the provider:: prefix

Built-in HCL functions are implemented inside Terraform CLI itself and are always available, regardless of which providers are used; provider-defined functions are implemented and shipped by the PROVIDER ITSELF (for example, hashicorp/aws can add its own specific function) and are only available if the corresponding provider is declared in required_providers — this lets providers extend the set of available functions without modifying Terraform's core
provider-defined functions can only be used inside a provider block, not in locals/resource
provider::aws::arn_parse is not a function but an alias for a data source
explanation: Provider-defined functions (starting with Terraform 1.8, requiring the Plugin Framework on the provider's side) are a mechanism allowing provider authors to ship their own functions, invoked via the syntax provider::<provider_name>::<function_name>(...) — unlike built-in HCL functions, which are part of the language itself and don't depend on which providers are connected in the configuration.

question: In HCP Terraform, for a VCS-driven workspace, a plan is automatically triggered on a Pull Request, but applying on the main branch requires manual confirmation in the UI. What is this type of plan called, run on a PR and not leading to any actual infrastructure change?
options: Destructive plan

Speculative plan — a special type of run that computes a plan of changes (for example, to preview it in a PR comment), but which fundamentally CANNOT be applied (there's no corresponding apply button/action) — used specifically for code review before merging, unlike a normal plan+apply run on the main branch
Dry-run apply — equivalent to apply, but without actually applying it to the provider's API
Shadow plan — a second plan run in parallel with the main one for cross-checking results

options: It entirely eliminates the need to write a resource block by hand: Terraform ITSELF generates a starting configuration (a set of resource attributes) based on the real state of the imported resource and writes it to the specified file — after which an engineer typically reviews/refines the generated code before committing it
It is used only to generate output.tf files, not resource configuration
The flag only works with resources that already have a corresponding resource block in code — otherwise it errors out
-generate-config-out is only available in HCP Terraform (Cloud), not in the open-source CLI
explanation: terraform plan -generate-config-out=<file>, used together with an import block that does NOT yet have a corresponding resource block in code, generates starter HCL configuration based on the real resource's data at the provider and writes it to the specified file. This significantly simplifies migrating existing, manually created infrastructure under Terraform management — no need to write resource attributes by hand from scratch, though the generated code usually needs review/cleanup (e.g. replacing hardcoded values with variables).

question: Starting with Terraform 1.10, a new type of configuration block appeared — the ephemeral resource. What is its fundamental difference from an ordinary resource?
options: An ephemeral resource is simply a renamed synonym for a data source for new providers, with no functional difference

Values obtained from an ephemeral resource EXIST ONLY during a single plan/apply run and are NEVER saved to the state file — they are meant for transient data (e.g. short-lived tokens/credentials) that should not be stored long-term anywhere on disk
An ephemeral resource is always recreated on every apply, like a regular resource with no lifecycle restrictions
An ephemeral resource can only be used inside provisioner blocks, not as a value for resource attributes
explanation: Ephemeral resources (Terraform 1.10+) are a new type of block (a `resource` with an `ephemeral` modifier / a separate `ephemeral` block, depending on the provider) whose values exist only in memory within a single plan/apply run and are fundamentally NOT persisted to the state file. This is specifically designed for secrets/tokens whose lifetime should be minimized, reducing the risk of their long-term storage in plain or encrypted state.

question:
Given the code:
```
variable "session_token" {
  type      = string
  ephemeral = true
}
```
What does the ephemeral = true attribute mean for a variable declaration (Terraform 1.10+)?
options: It is identical to sensitive = true and simply hides the value from CLI output

It marks the VARIABLE ITSELF as ephemeral: its value is available only during the current run (plan/apply) and CANNOT be used anywhere the value must persist between runs (e.g. directly as a regular attribute of a persistent resource that ends up in state) — Terraform statically checks for and forbids such 'leakage' of an ephemeral value into permanently stored locations
ephemeral = true makes the variable temporary only for the current terraform workspace, automatically removing it when the workspace is switched
The ephemeral attribute is only available for output blocks, not for variable
explanation: A variable with ephemeral = true (Terraform 1.10+) can only be used in contexts that don't require the value to persist between runs (e.g. passed into a provider authentication block, into an ephemeral resource, into a write-only argument) — Terraform statically checks the usage graph and prevents such a value from being assigned to an ordinary persisted resource attribute, guarding against accidentally leaking a transient value into state.

question: Terraform 1.11 introduced the concept of a write-only argument for some resource attributes. What does this mean?
options: A write-only argument is a value that Terraform passes to the provider on apply (a write), but fundamentally does NOT save or read back from state — meaning on the next plan Terraform has no saved value of this attribute to compare against, which is specifically designed for secrets that should never be stored in state in any form long-term
Write-only means the attribute can only be set once at create time, and cannot be changed afterward (any change forces recreation)
Write-only arguments are only available inside provisioner blocks, never in the resource itself
Write-only is a deprecated name for computed attributes calculated by the provider
explanation: Write-only arguments (Terraform 1.11+, requires provider-side support via the Plugin Framework) are a special attribute type whose value is passed to the provider on apply, but never saved or read back from state. This complements the sensitive/ephemeral approach to secrets: even an encrypted state won't contain the actual value of such an attribute at all, reducing the exposure surface if the state file itself is ever compromised.

question: What is the `terraform console` command for?
options: It opens an interactive REPL in which you can evaluate arbitrary HCL expressions (including references to existing resources/variables/locals of the current configuration via the actual state) — useful for debugging functions and expressions without running a full plan/apply
It opens an SSH session directly into one of the virtual servers Terraform created
It connects to the provider's own console (e.g. AWS CloudShell) using the credentials configured in the provider block
The command is only available in HCP Terraform (Cloud), not in the open-source CLI
explanation: terraform console opens an interactive REPL for the current working directory/workspace: you can type arbitrary HCL expressions (function calls, references to var./local./data./resource attributes from the current state) and immediately see the evaluated result — extremely useful for quickly checking how a specific function (e.g. cidrsubnet() or regex()) behaves without needing to run a full apply.

question: What does the `terraform graph` command do?
options: It outputs a text (DOT-format, for Graphviz) representation of the dependency graph of resources/modules/data sources in the current configuration — useful for visualizing create/destroy ordering and spotting unexpected dependencies
It builds and immediately opens an interactive web dashboard with cloud resource usage metrics in the browser
It is equivalent to terraform plan, but with a more compact tabular output of changes
graph is a command available only within the HCP Terraform UI, not in the CLI
explanation: terraform graph outputs a dependency graph (in DOT format, suitable for conversion via Graphviz's `dot` into PNG/SVG) — nodes represent resources/modules/data sources/outputs, and edges represent dependencies between them. This is a purely diagnostic tool for understanding operation ordering and debugging unexpected implicit dependencies; it has no effect on the actual plan of changes.

question: What is the `terraform add` command for?
options: It generates an HCL resource block template for the given resource type (optionally — based on a real existing resource via `-from-state`), which is convenient as a starting point when writing configuration from scratch or preparing for an import
It automatically adds a new provider to the required_providers section
It physically creates a new resource in the cloud immediately, bypassing plan/apply
terraform add is a synonym for terraform init, simply a newer name for the command
explanation: terraform add <type>.<name> generates a resource block 'skeleton' listing all attributes known to the provider (usually with placeholder values) — a convenient starting point for writing configuration. The `-from-state` flag lets you generate the block based on the values of an already-existing resource in state (e.g. as an alternative/complement to `-generate-config-out` when working with import).

question: How does `terraform show -json` differ from plain `terraform show`?
options: -json outputs the CONTENT OF THE STATE (or a saved plan file, if a path to one is given) in machine-readable JSON format instead of human-readable text — used for programmatic integration (e.g. analyzing resources with third-party tools like Infracost, OPA/conftest) instead of parsing unstable text output
-json only works with saved plans (via -out), and cannot show the current state
terraform show -json is unavailable without first configuring a remote backend
-json is fully identical to regular show, simply wrapping the same text in a JSON string
explanation: terraform show [path_to_state_or_plan] -json outputs a structured, documented, and cross-release-versioned JSON representation of the state or a saved plan file — the official way to integrate third-party tools (policy engines, cost analysis, visualization), unlike the text output without the flag, whose format isn't guaranteed and isn't meant to be parsed.

question: The `terraform taint <address>` command is considered deprecated. What modern approach has replaced it?
options: The `-replace=<address>` flag on terraform plan/apply commands — it achieves the same effect (forcing a specific resource to be recreated on the next apply), but is explicitly specified on each run (rather than persisted as a hidden marker in state that's easy to forget), and is visible directly in the plan output as an explicit intent
Completely removing the resource from the configuration code, which triggers automatic recreation
The taint command was not replaced by anything — it was simply removed with no alternative
The force_recreate = true attribute inside a lifecycle block
explanation: terraform taint marked a resource in state as 'tainted' (a persisted flag), causing it to be recreated on the NEXT apply — the problem was that this marker was implicit, living in state separately from the invocation itself, and easy to forget/lose track of. The `-replace=<address>` flag on plan/apply solves the same problem explicitly and on a one-time basis for each specific run, with no hidden mutating state — this is the recommended modern approach.

question: What is the `TF_DATA_DIR` environment variable used for?
options: It overrides the path to the hidden `.terraform` working directory (provider plugins, modules, lock file cache) — by default `.terraform` is created alongside the code, but TF_DATA_DIR lets you place it elsewhere (useful, e.g., for running the same configuration in parallel in different CI jobs without cache conflicts)
It specifies the path where the final state file is saved instead of the standard terraform.tfstate
TF_DATA_DIR sets the directory for .tfvars files automatically loaded at startup
The variable is only used to specify the path to the terraform CLI binary itself
explanation: TF_DATA_DIR overrides the location of the internal `.terraform` working directory (provider/module cache; the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file is created separately alongside the code, but the plugin structure itself lives in the data dir) — instead of the default `<cwd>/.terraform`. This is useful for isolating parallel runs of the same configuration (e.g. CI matrix jobs over the same code with different variables), preventing them from sharing one plugin cache.

question: What is the `TF_CLI_ARGS_plan` environment variable used for?
options: It lets you specify ADDITIONAL command-line arguments that Terraform will automatically append to EVERY invocation of the `plan` command specifically (the suffix after the underscore names the specific subcommand) — e.g. `TF_CLI_ARGS_plan="-input=false"` avoids having to add this flag manually on every plan invocation
It sets arguments applied ONLY to the apply command, regardless of the suffix in the variable's name
TF_CLI_ARGS_plan overrides the search path used to find the terraform binary itself for running plan
TF_CLI_ARGS_* variables are only supported in HCP Terraform Agents, not in the regular CLI
explanation: TF_CLI_ARGS (without a suffix) adds arguments to ANY terraform command, while TF_CLI_ARGS_<subcommand> (e.g. TF_CLI_ARGS_plan, TF_CLI_ARGS_apply) adds them only to that specific subcommand. This is convenient for setting environment-wide default flags (e.g. disabling interactive input in CI via -input=false) without having to edit the invocations themselves in every script.

question: With the local backend, Terraform automatically creates a `terraform.tfstate.backup` file. What is stored in it?
options: A copy of the state file as it looked IMMEDIATELY BEFORE the last successful apply — i.e. the previous version of the state — this backup is created automatically before every overwrite of terraform.tfstate, allowing a manual rollback to the previous state if something goes wrong
An encrypted copy of all credentials used by providers during the last apply
A full log of CLI commands executed over the last 30 days
The .backup file is only created when using a remote backend, never with a local one
explanation: With the local backend, Terraform automatically saves the PREVIOUS version of the file as terraform.tfstate.backup right before every overwrite of terraform.tfstate — a simple built-in safeguard against losing state, letting you manually restore the previous state if a new apply produces an undesirable result. Most remote backends have their own, more advanced state-versioning mechanisms (e.g. S3 object versioning), so this .backup file is specific to the local backend.

question: What is the `-compact-warnings` flag used for on plan/apply/validate commands?
options: It completely disables printing all warning messages, showing only errors

It shortens the multi-line detailed output of EACH warning message down to a single summary line per file/source (aggregating repeated warnings), which is useful when a configuration produces many similar warnings whose full text would clutter a CI log
-compact-warnings turns warning messages into errors, halting execution
The flag only works together with -json and has no effect on regular text output
explanation: -compact-warnings shortens the detailed (often multi-line, with an exact code range) output of each warning down to a compact summary line — the warnings themselves are not removed or ignored, only their textual representation becomes much shorter, which is useful in CI logs where many similar deprecation warnings could otherwise clutter the main output.

question: How does `terraform fmt -check -recursive` differ from plain `terraform fmt`?
options: -check makes the command only REPORT (via a list of files and a non-zero exit code if there are discrepancies) WITHOUT MODIFYING files on disk, and -recursive extends the check to all NESTED subdirectories (including modules), not just the current directory — a typical use case is a CI gate checking code style without the side effect of automatically reformatting files
-check is fully equivalent to plain fmt, just with more verbose change logging
-recursive without -check automatically deletes all .tf files that fail formatting
The -check and -recursive flags are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together
explanation: Plain terraform fmt rewrites files on disk in the canonical formatting style. The -check flag changes the behavior to 'check only': the command does not modify files, and returns a list of non-conforming files plus a non-zero exit code if any deviations exist — which makes it convenient as a CI gate (fail the build on unformatted code). -recursive extends the traversal from the current directory to all subdirectories (e.g. nested module directories).

question: What is the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file, created after `terraform init`, used for?
options: It records the EXACT versions and cryptographic hashes (checksums) of every provider used in the project, ensuring reproducibility: a subsequent `terraform init` (e.g. on a different machine or in CI) will use EXACTLY the same provider versions and verify their integrity via hash, rather than just 'any version matching the range' — the file is recommended to be committed to git alongside the code itself
It locks the state file against simultaneous modification by multiple users (state locking) — i.e. it plays the same role that a DynamoDB table plays for the S3 backend
.terraform.lock.hcl is a temporary file created only for the duration of a single command and deleted immediately after it completes
The file is only needed when using modules from the Terraform Registry, not when using providers
explanation: The provider lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl) records the selected provider versions along with distribution hashes for various platforms — a mechanism separate from state locking (which ensures no two applies run concurrently). Committing it to git guarantees that the whole team and CI use identical provider versions, rather than just 'something satisfying the version range' from required_providers, which reduces the risk of unexpected behavior differences between machines.

question: What is the `-json` flag on the `terraform version` command useful for?
options: terraform version -json outputs the Terraform CLI version itself, platform (OS/arch) details, and the versions of ALL providers in use, in structured JSON format — useful for programmatically checking versions in CI scripts (e.g. a gate on a minimum required version) without parsing regular human-readable text
-json shows only the Terraform CLI version and does not include provider versions, unlike a plain invocation without the flag
The -json flag on version is unavailable — version only supports text output
terraform version -json requires prior authentication with HCP Terraform
explanation: terraform version -json returns a structured JSON object with fields such as terraform_version, platform, and provider_selections (the versions of all providers pinned in the current .terraform.lock.hcl) — useful for automated CI checks (e.g. a script that requires a specific minimum Terraform version or a specific provider version before running the main pipeline), rather than parsing unstructured plain-text output from regular `terraform version`.
